problem: Existing LLM-based robot navigation approaches do not work well outdoors with open-set objects and free-form instructions. Some turn detector outputs into text-only scene descriptions for LLM reasoning, which loses visual and spatial detail and inherits detector errors (LLM-TG). Others use LLMs only as high-level planners that call predefined motion primitives, or rely on task-specific in-context examples (VoxPoser, SayCan).
motivation: Outdoor, unstructured navigation needs disambiguation using fine-grained visual cues (color, shape, spatial relations), and it needs low-level trajectories that are both instruction-shaped and collision-free. The authors observe that MLLMs have strong cross-modal scene understanding and code-generation ability. They also observe that MLLMs lack geometric grounding and produce colliding trajectories. This motivates coupling the MLLM with a LiDAR-based open-vocabulary perception system and a classical planner.
key_idea: A frozen GPT-4o is driven by a single task-agnostic prompt, sees an annotated RGB image plus per-object text attributes, and writes and self-debugs Python code for a coarse, instruction-aligned trajectory. That trajectory is used to lower costs in a BEV value map built from occupancy and semantics, and A* then refines it into a geometry-compliant, collision-free path.
insight:
Two lessons come out of the experiments.

1. Visual input to the MLLM matters when instructions are ambiguous. With the same GPT-4o and only the input modality changed, the text-only LLM-TG falls to 13/50 on ambiguous tasks, while OpenNav gets 42/50. The annotated image lets the MLLM notice detector mistakes, e.g. a cylindrical building captioned as a trash bin.
2. MLLM spatial reasoning and geometric planning complement each other. In the trajectory ablation (Table II), A* alone never collides (0/30) but ignores instruction shape (NDTW 0.08). MLLM-only code trajectories (VLT-Code) follow intent better (NDTW 0.16) but collide 16/30. Using the MLLM trajectory as a cost prior for A* gives the best result on both (NDTW 0.38, Fréchet 12.60, 2/30 collisions).
method: Task-agnostic system prompt: one prompt with five parts. These are available functions (det_object(), A_star_plan(start,end), visual_3D(traj)), an environment description (coordinate frame, robot pose, sensors), collision-avoidance guidance, step-by-step initial planning/decomposition, and a code-generation instruction to produce the trajectory in segments. No in-context examples or motion primitives are used.

Open Vocabulary Perception System (OVPS, built on OpenGraph): RAM tags categories, Grounding DINO detects boxes, and TAP (Tokenize Anything via Prompting) segments and captions each object. LiDAR points are projected into the masks via the camera intrinsics/extrinsics (M_K M_T) to get per-object 3D points, center pose, dimensions and the nearest reachable point (NRP) on each drivable region.

Multimodal MLLM interface: GPT-4o receives text entries (caption, position, size, NRP dictionary, numeric ID) plus an RGB image with object contours colored and labeled by the same IDs. This lets it cross-check captions against the visual evidence and resolve spatial references such as 'on your right'.

Code-as-trajectory with self-debugging: the MLLM reasons about the trajectory shape (start, intermediate waypoints near relevant objects, end at the NRP of the target) and writes a Python script. The script is executed, and on exception the error message is fed back so the MLLM can debug and re-run until a dense 3D trajectory is produced (Algorithm 1 loop).

BEV value map + A* refinement: occupied cells get high cost, and non-selected ground regions also get high cost. The chosen drivable region gets a slightly higher cost than cells within a radius of the MLLM's coarse trajectory, which get the lowest cost. A* is run on this value map and the result is B-spline smoothed into [x, y, z, heading] waypoints.

setting.backbone: GPT-4o (ChatGPT-4o, frozen, zero-shot) as planner/code generator; frozen perception models RAM + Grounding DINO + TAP (OpenGraph pipeline); classical A* planner
setting.observation: posed RGB images + 3D LiDAR point clouds (SemanticKITTI); the MLLM receives an annotated RGB image plus text object attributes (caption, position, size, nearest reachable points)
setting.action_space: dense trajectory waypoints [x, y, z, heading]: MLLM code-generated coarse waypoints refined by A* on a 2D BEV value map, then B-spline smoothed
setting.simulator: none: offline evaluation on the SemanticKITTI autonomous-driving dataset (sequence 05); real-world Clearpath Husky demos
setting.privileged: dataset poses for LiDAR-camera fusion and a reconstructed 3D map / BEV occupancy + semantic map of the scene from the posed sensor data (planning is on a pre-built map, not online exploration)

numbers.extra: Custom benchmark of 150 instructions (50 specific, 50 ambiguous, 50 high-level reasoning) on SemanticKITTI sequence 05; success = final position within 1 m of the GT endpoint; the only baseline is LLM-TG with the same GPT-4o
numbers.evidence: Table I 'Performance comparison of LLM-TG and OpenNav. SR: Success Rate, NE: Navigation Error.' Total row: 1.68 / 84%

numbers.extra: Custom evaluation against user-drawn trajectories ('ten selected task scenarios', collisions reported over 30); NDTW printed as 0.38 and converted to 0-100
numbers.evidence: Table II 'Performance in Trajectory Synthesis': OpenNav 12.60 / 0.38 / 2/30

numbers.method: VLT-Code (ablation: MLLM code trajectory without value map / A* refinement)

numbers_note:
Evaluation uses only custom, small-scale benchmarks on SemanticKITTI sequence 05; no standard VLN benchmarks (R2R, R2R-CE, etc.) are reported. Table I gives per-category SR as counts (e.g. 45/50); these are copied as strings, with the total SR printed as 84%. There are inconsistencies:
- The text says both methods achieve '100% success rate' on unambiguous tasks, but Table I shows 43/50 and 45/50.
- The trajectory experiment mentions 'ten selected task scenarios' while collisions are reported out of 30.
The NDTW values in Table II (0.38, 0.16) were converted to 38 and 16. Real-robot results are qualitative only (project website).
results: On 150 custom SemanticKITTI navigation instructions, OpenNav reaches 84% SR and 1.68 NE, versus 53% SR and 4.91 NE for the text-only LLM-TG baseline using the same GPT-4o. The gap is largest on ambiguous object references (42/50 vs 13/50) and high-level reasoning instructions (40/50 vs 23/50). In trajectory-shape alignment with user-drawn paths, OpenNav gets Fréchet 12.60, NDTW 0.38 and 2/30 collisions. This beats A* (24.20 / 0.08 / 0/30) and MLLM-only code trajectories (17.53 / 0.16 / 16/30).
limitations: Very small, custom evaluation: one SemanticKITTI sequence, 150 author-designed instructions and a handful of trajectory scenarios, with a single baseline (LLM-TG). There are no standard VLN benchmarks, and real-robot results are qualitative only.
Open-loop, single-shot planning on a static reconstructed map built from posed sensor data. There is no online exploration or closed-loop replanning, and dynamic environments are left to future work.
Relies on a proprietary MLLM (GPT-4o) and a heavy multi-model perception stack (RAM + Grounding DINO + TAP + LiDAR fusion). Latency and cost are not reported.
builds_on: LLM-TG (Kwon et al., Language Models as Zero-Shot Trajectory Generators)
